title: The Browser and the Manifesto: from New Lisbon to Sand Hill Road
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: New Lisbon: A Town, a Terminal, a Missing Teacher

stops.name: Cedar Falls, the birth
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day. The University of Illinois Distributed Museum exhibit page on Andreessen (distributedmuseum.illinois.edu, fetched directly in research) and Wikipedia, 'Marc Andreessen', both give 9 July 1971 at Cedar Falls, Iowa. No source consulted names a hospital, so the pin is the city, not a building.
stops.campa: Marc Lowell Andreessen is born at Cedar Falls, Iowa, on the ninth of July, 1971, in the corn country of the upper Midwest, four hundred miles from any ocean. The family will move north into Wisconsin while he is still small. Nothing in the town or the year marks the child out, and the record of his first decade is the ordinary record of a Midwestern boy, which is to say almost none at all. The exhibit page the University of Illinois will one day build for him opens on this line and this date. No source consulted names the hospital.
sources: University of Illinois Distributed Museum, exhibit page on Marc Andreessen
suggested_refs: The Distributed Museum exhibit page at the University of Illinois, which opens the record of his life at this date

stops.name: New Lisbon, the town and the library book
stops.date_confidence: The New Lisbon boyhood is attested (Wikipedia, 'Marc Andreessen'). That he began programming around age twelve is Wikipedia's, citing later profiles; the characterization of the school culture comes from Tad Friend's 2015 New Yorker profile as relayed in the research dossier, the magazine itself paywalled and not fetched this session. The date is a placeholder for 'around twelve'; month and day are defaults. Coordinates corrected from the research pool's 43.8739, -90.1806, which falls about 1.3 km southwest of the town, to the Nominatim value for New Lisbon, Juneau County.
stops.campa: New Lisbon, Juneau County, Wisconsin: a rural town of a few thousand where the school's weather is athletics, and the boy is not an athlete. He reads instead. At about twelve he teaches himself to program, working from a library book. Profiles written about him twenty years later keep returning to this town for an explanation, and what they find in it is a bright unathletic child and a set of tools nobody around him is using. The nearest software industry is five hundred miles east. He goes on reading.
sources: Tad Friend, 'Tomorrow's Advance Man', The New Yorker, 2015 (via the Marc Andreessen research dossier; paywalled and not fetched)
suggested_refs: New Lisbon High School and the Juneau County public library system in the early 1980s

stops.name: New Lisbon, the teacher who did not come home
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction on the date, attested on the substance. That Andreessen's former New Lisbon High School teacher Barbara Blackstone disappeared and was found murdered, and that Andreessen later offered a $25,000 reward, is stated on Wikipedia, 'Marc Andreessen'. The specific date of 9 July 1987, and with it the coincidence that it falls on Andreessen's sixteenth birthday, rests only on dossier-cited local reporting that was not independently fetched this session. The coincidence should not be repeated as fact without that reporting in hand.
stops.campa: Barbara Blackstone taught at New Lisbon High School. In the summer of 1987 she disappears; she is later found murdered, and the case is not solved. Andreessen is fifteen or sixteen, one of her students, and the town he leaves for Illinois two years later is a town with an open killing in it. Twenty-two years later, from California, he will put twenty-five thousand dollars of his own money behind information leading to a conviction. The case is still open.
sources: Local Juneau County reporting on the Blackstone case, cited in the Marc Andreessen research dossier and not independently fetched
suggested_refs: The unsolved 1987 murder of Barbara Blackstone, New Lisbon, Wisconsin

segments.name: Urbana: The Browser Made by Hourly Labor

stops.name: Urbana-Champaign, the computer science degree
stops.date_confidence: Attested that he studied computer science at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and completed the degree in December 1993 (Wikipedia, 'Marc Andreessen'; University of Illinois Distributed Museum). The 1989 start is inferred from the December 1993 completion and is an ordering device; month and day are defaults. The pin is the Grainger Engineering Library, which the Distributed Museum names as the site of the poster later hung for him in its Engineering Hall of Fame.
stops.campa: He enrolls at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, a land-grant campus in the flat middle of the state that happens, for reasons of federal supercomputing money, to hold one of the best-connected buildings in the country. He will take four and a half years over the degree and finish it in December 1993, by which time the thing he made in the basement is already famous and he is already gone. The Grainger Engineering Library eventually hangs his poster in its hall of fame.
sources: University of Illinois Distributed Museum, exhibit page on Marc Andreessen
suggested_refs: The Grainger Engineering Library Engineering Hall of Fame poster for Marc Andreessen

stops.name: Austin, two summers inside IBM
stops.date_confidence: Attested that he interned at IBM in Austin, Texas, as an undergraduate, and Wikipedia says twice, not once. The year is unsourced: the 1995 Smithsonian oral history that the dossier dates the work to (americanhistory.si.edu/comphist/ma1.html) returned HTTP 403 this session and web.archive.org was unreachable, so 1990 is an ordering device only, with month and day defaults. Coordinates corrected from the pool's 30.3898, -97.7038, about 1.9 km east of the campus, to IBM Building 045, 11400 Burnet Road, per Nominatim.
stops.campa: Twice as an undergraduate he goes down to Austin on IBM's dime and works inside the largest computer company on earth, in the graphics and workstation end of it, at the exact moment that end of it is losing. He sees how a corporation of four hundred thousand people decides what to build, and how long the deciding takes. Everything he does afterward is done fast and by four people. The oral history in which he describes these summers is now behind a server that returns a refusal, so the account of what he learned there is his own and secondhand.
sources: Smithsonian National Museum of American History, oral history with Marc Andreessen, June 1995 (page returned HTTP 403; summarized via the research dossier)
suggested_refs: IBM's Austin workstation and 3D graphics operations, c. 1990

stops.name: NCSA, hired by the hour
stops.date_confidence: Attested that Andreessen worked as an hourly student programmer at the National Center for Supercomputing Applications while an undergraduate (Wikipedia, 'Marc Andreessen'). The 1992 start is the dossier's and Wikipedia's, without a month; month and day are defaults. Coordinates corrected from the pool's 40.1095, -88.2287, roughly 630 m south-southwest of the building, to the Nominatim value for NCSA, 1205 West Clark Street, Urbana.
stops.campa: The National Center for Supercomputing Applications at 1205 West Clark Street exists because Congress decided the country needed public supercomputers, and it staffs its edges with undergraduates paid by the hour. Andreessen is one of them, and the terms of an hourly job are that anything he writes on the clock belongs to the university. The federal network runs into this building. So does the specification Tim Berners-Lee has published out of CERN, which almost nobody in the United States is reading. He reads it.
sources: University of Illinois Distributed Museum, exhibit page on Marc Andreessen
suggested_refs: The NCSA building at 1205 West Clark Street, Urbana, and the historical marker later placed at its south entrance

stops.name: NCSA, Mosaic and the picture inside the page
stops.date_confidence: Attested. The University of Illinois Distributed Museum dates the initial Mosaic release and announcement to 23 January 1993, with Macintosh and Windows ports later that year; Wikipedia and the Internet Hall of Fame citation both confirm authorship with Eric Bina at NCSA. Same corrected NCSA coordinates as the previous stop.
stops.campa: With Eric Bina, a staff programmer at the same center, he writes NCSA Mosaic. Other browsers exist; this one puts the image inline in the page instead of opening it in a separate window, installs on a Macintosh and on Windows as well as on Unix, and can be used by a person who has never heard the word protocol. The two of them ship it on the twenty-third of January, 1993, and put it out for free. Within a year the number of people looking at the web goes from thousands to millions.
stops.quote: the first widely used Web browser
stops.quote_source: Internet Hall of Fame, official induction citation for Marc Andreessen, 2013
sources: University of Illinois Distributed Museum, exhibit page on Marc Andreessen
Internet Hall of Fame, induction citation, internethalloffame.org
Marc Andreessen and Eric Bina, 'NCSA Mosaic: A Global Hypermedia System', Internet Research 4:1 (1994), pp. 7-17, DOI 10.1108/10662249410798803
suggested_refs: The Andreessen and Bina paper in Internet Research, vol. 4 no. 1 (1994), the authors' own technical account of the browser
github.com/alandipert/ncsa-mosaic, Alan Dipert's buildable port of Mosaic 2.7 to modern systems

segments.name: Mountain View: The Company Named Twice

stops.name: Palo Alto, three months at Enterprise Integration Technologies
stops.date_confidence: Attested that after the University of Illinois he moved to California and worked at Enterprise Integration Technologies, and that EIT was based in Palo Alto (Wikipedia, 'Marc Andreessen'; New York Times, 13 April 1994, 'Enterprise Integration Technologies, based in Palo Alto, Calif.'). The research pool dated this to October 1993, but the degree was completed in December 1993, so the pool's own dating is inconsistent; corrected here to late 1993 with a default day. The 'about three months' figure and the October visit rest solely on the Smithsonian oral history, which returned HTTP 403. EIT's street address was not located, so the pin is the city.
stops.campa: The degree is finished in December and he goes west, to a small Palo Alto firm working on commercial transactions over the network. He is twenty-two, he has written the software a million people are using, he owns none of it, and he is drawing a salary from somebody else in a valley that has not yet worked out what he is worth. The job lasts about three months by his own later account, and that account is the only source there is for it; the interview it comes from now returns a refusal from the server.
sources: New York Times, 13 April 1994 (EIT located in Palo Alto)
Smithsonian National Museum of American History, oral history with Marc Andreessen, June 1995 (HTTP 403; via the research dossier)
suggested_refs: Enterprise Integration Technologies, Palo Alto, and its early work on commercial transaction protocols

stops.name: Mountain View, Mosaic Communications Corporation founded
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day: Wikipedia, 'Netscape', gives 4 April 1994 for the founding of Mosaic Communications Corporation. The meeting with Jim Clark, then leaving Silicon Graphics, is attested (Wikipedia, 'Marc Andreessen'), but no source fetched fixes a venue or a date for their first conversation, and the interactive-television detour in their early talks comes from the dossier's narrative alone. Coordinates corrected from the research pool's 37.4104, -122.0673, which matches neither address: in 1994 the company occupied 650 Castro Street, Mountain View, used here.
stops.campa: Jim Clark has just left Silicon Graphics, the company he founded, with money and no project. He hears about the browser and writes to the boy who made it. Their first conversations wander through interactive television before landing where Andreessen wants them: a commercial browser, written from scratch, sold as a product. They incorporate as Mosaic Communications Corporation on the fourth of April, 1994. Andreessen goes back to Illinois and hires five or six of the people he worked beside at the center.
sources: Marc Andreessen research dossier (Clark's approach and the early conversations)
suggested_refs: 650 Castro Street, Mountain View, the company's first offices

stops.name: Mountain View, Navigator ships
stops.date_confidence: Attested that Netscape Navigator was released in October 1994 and that Andreessen was a co-founder holding executive and technical titles later summarized in SEC filings as Chief Technology Officer and Executive Vice President of Products. The specific day, 13 October, is the conventional release date and is not confirmed by any source fetched this session; treat the month as firm and the day as a default within it. Same 650 Castro Street pin as the founding.
stops.campa: Six months after incorporation the new browser goes out over the network it is built to read, free to individuals, and it is faster than Mosaic and better than Mosaic and written by the same hands that wrote Mosaic without using a line of its code. Andreessen is twenty-three and holds titles a corporate lawyer will later have to summarize for the Securities and Exchange Commission. The download is the distribution: no box, no disk, no shelf, no distributor taking a cut.
sources: Netscape SEC filings on officer titles, cited in the research dossier
suggested_refs: Netscape Navigator 1.0 and its free-for-individuals distribution model

stops.name: Mountain View, the name given back
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day: Wikipedia, 'Netscape', gives 14 November 1994 for the change of corporate name to Netscape Communications Corporation, made to end the trademark conflict with the University of Illinois and NCSA. The research pool collapsed the founding and the renaming into a bare '1994'; they are separated here.
stops.campa: The University of Illinois objects. The name Mosaic belongs to the building on West Clark Street and to the federal money that paid for it, not to the undergraduate who was on the clock. On the fourteenth of November the company gives the name up and becomes Netscape Communications Corporation. The university keeps the word and licenses its own browser to a competitor; the company keeps the people, the code written second, and the market. Whoever drafted the hourly employment terms in Urbana had been right about the ownership and wrong about what was worth owning.
suggested_refs: The NCSA trademark dispute over the Mosaic name, 1994

stops.name: Mountain View, forty bits for export
stops.date_confidence: Attested that Netscape shipped a domestic build and a deliberately weakened forty-bit export build under United States munitions law, and that cypherpunks including Hal Finney set out to break the export build; the atlas's own hal_finney.journey.json carries this at its stop 'Mountain View, forty bits for export', dating it to 1994 from Wikipedia, 'Damien Doligez', with month and day defaulted. Andreessen is not named in that file and is not on record in any source fetched this session on the export decision, which was the company's. The date here is a default late in 1994; the pin is Netscape's own 1994 address rather than Finney's location.
stops.campa: American law counts strong cryptography as a munition, so the company ships two browsers: one for Americans and one for everybody else, with the key cut to forty bits. It is Netscape's commerce that the weak key is supposed to protect, and Netscape's product that the government has decided to keep breakable. Hal Finney and the other cypherpunks read the regulation as a claim about arithmetic and set out to check it. They are right, and the export build falls. No source consulted puts Andreessen anywhere near the decision to ship it; the decision was the company's, and the company is eight months old.
sources: working/journeys/hal_finney.journey.json, stop 'Mountain View, forty bits for export'
suggested_refs: The ITAR export regulations on cryptography as they stood in 1994
Hal Finney's cypherpunk challenge against Netscape's forty-bit export build

segments.name: The Offering and the Browser War

stops.name: Mountain View, the meeting of the twenty-first of June
stops.date_confidence: Attested that a meeting between Microsoft and Netscape took place on 21 June 1995 and that Netscape witnesses testified it included proposals to divide the browser market, and that this meeting became central evidence in United States v. Microsoft. The justice.gov and cyber.harvard.edu trial archives were not fetched this session, and no source fetched names who sat in the room for Netscape, so Andreessen's presence at the table is not established here. The pin is Netscape's headquarters at 501 East Middlefield Road, corrected from the pool's 37.4104, -122.0673, which matches no Netscape address; the trial itself was held at the E. Barrett Prettyman courthouse in Washington and is cited below rather than staged as a stop.
stops.campa: Microsoft comes to Netscape in June and proposes an arrangement. What was said in that room is disputed for the next six years in a federal courtroom in Washington, where the government argues that the proposal was a division of the market: Microsoft to take the Windows browser, Netscape to take everything else, and the operating system to remain untouchable. Netscape declines. No source consulted names who sat at that table for Netscape. Within a year Internet Explorer is bundled into Windows and given away free with every machine sold.
sources: United States v. Microsoft trial record, cited in the Marc Andreessen research dossier (justice.gov and cyber.harvard.edu not fetched this session)
suggested_refs: The E. Barrett Prettyman United States Courthouse, Washington, where United States v. Microsoft was tried, 1998-2001
The 21 June 1995 Microsoft-Netscape meeting notes entered into the trial record

stops.name: Mountain View, the ninth of August
stops.date_confidence: Attested. Wikipedia, 'Netscape', confirms the mechanics: five million shares offered at $28, trading as high as roughly $75, closing at $58.25, valuing the company near $2.9 billion at the close. The listing was a Nasdaq event with no single physical site; the pin is Netscape's Mountain View headquarters at 501 East Middlefield Road, corrected from the pool's 37.4104, -122.0673, and stands for where Andreessen was based that day rather than for anywhere the trading happened.
stops.campa: Netscape goes public sixteen months after incorporation, with a product given away free and no profits. Five million shares are offered at twenty-eight dollars. The stock opens at more than double that, runs to seventy-five, and closes at fifty-eight and a quarter. The company is worth something near three billion dollars by the closing bell and Andreessen, twenty-four years old, is rich in an afternoon. Everything the following five years does to American capital, the dot-com boom entire, starts on this date with this offering.
suggested_refs: The Netscape Communications initial public offering, 9 August 1995, conventionally dated as the opening of the dot-com era

stops.name: Time and Life Building, the barefoot king
stops.date_confidence: Attested as to the cover and its content: Wikipedia, 'Marc Andreessen', describes the Time cover of 19 February 1996, 'The Golden Geeks', showing Andreessen barefoot and wearing a crown on a throne-like chair. The photographer is not named in any source fetched, and no source places Andreessen in New York for the sitting; the pin is Time's own address at 1271 Avenue of the Americas, corrected from the pool's 40.7128, -74.006, which is lower Manhattan, and it stands for the magazine rather than for anywhere he was.
stops.campa: Time puts him on the cover of the nineteenth of February, 1996, seated on a throne with a crown on his head and no shoes on his feet, under the words The Golden Geeks. He is twenty-four. The picture is a joke about a boy king and it is also entirely serious, and it fixes the type: the programmer as sovereign, barefoot because he does not have to dress for anyone. Every profile of a young technology billionaire written for the next thirty years is working against this photograph or copying it. The photographer is not named.
suggested_refs: Time magazine cover, 19 February 1996, 'The Golden Geeks'

stops.name: Mountain View, the source given away
stops.date_confidence: Attested as to the announcement date: Wikipedia, 'Netscape', gives 22 January 1998 for the announcement that the browser source would be released, with the code following under the Netscape Public License in the weeks after (Wikipedia says February 1998; the mozilla.org drop is conventionally dated 31 March 1998). The research pool tagged the whole of 1998; the announcement is separated from the release here, and the release date itself is left as the disputed thing it is. Same corrected Middlefield Road pin.
stops.campa: Internet Explorer is free, bundled with the operating system, and installed on every new machine sold. Netscape's share of the browser market falls through the floor, the company announces a large loss and a restructuring, and on the twenty-second of January it announces the one thing nobody in the industry expects: the source code of the browser will be given away. The code goes out in the weeks that follow, under a licence written for the purpose, and the project that grows around it is called Mozilla.
suggested_refs: The Netscape Public License and the founding of mozilla.org, 1998

stops.name: Mountain View, sold to America Online
stops.date_confidence: Attested as to the announcement date of 24 November 1998. The price is a live contradiction and is not resolved here: Wikipedia, 'Marc Andreessen', gives $4.3 billion, other contemporaneous accounts about $4.2 billion at announcement, and retrospective accounts figures as high as roughly $10 billion, reflecting the rise in AOL's own stock between announcement and closing. All three numbers describe the same stock-for-stock transaction.
stops.campa: America Online announces it will buy Netscape in stock. The number reported at the announcement is four point three billion dollars; by the time the deal closes, AOL's own shares have run so far that retrospective accounts of the same transaction cite figures more than twice that, and the sources have never agreed since. Four years and seven months after Clark's first letter, the company is a line item in a dial-up subscription business. Andreessen is twenty-seven.
suggested_refs: The AOL-Netscape stock transaction and the disputed range of its reported value

segments.name: Dulles, the Cloud, and the Years of Building Companies

stops.name: Dulles, chief technology officer of America Online
stops.date_confidence: Attested that the AOL acquisition closed on 17 March 1999 (Wikipedia, 'Netscape') and that Andreessen became Chief Technology Officer of America Online (Wikipedia, 'Marc Andreessen'); the research pool's vague 'March 1999' is corrected to the day. The September 1999 resignation and the reported Virginia house near Dulles rest on the dossier's account; Wired's contemporaneous announcement (wired.com/1999/02/aol-names-andreessen-cto) could not be fetched this session.
stops.campa: The deal closes in March and the boy king becomes chief technology officer of America Online, in Dulles, Virginia, three thousand miles from the valley, inside a company whose business is charging households by the hour for a walled garden. He is reported to buy a house near the headquarters and to keep the California one. Nothing in the record suggests he was pushed, and nothing in it suggests he had anything to do there he wanted to do. He lasts about six months, and resigns in September.
sources: Marc Andreessen research dossier (AOL tenure and resignation)
suggested_refs: America Online's Dulles, Virginia campus at the height of the dial-up era

stops.name: Palo Alto, Loudcloud founded in the house
stops.date_confidence: Attested that Andreessen co-founded Loudcloud in 1999 with Ben Horowitz, Tim Howes, and In Sik Rhee (Wikipedia, 'Marc Andreessen'). That the founding conversations took place at Andreessen's own Palo Alto house is the dossier's narrative, not independently confirmed, and no address was located, so the pin is the city. September is chosen to follow the AOL resignation; the day is a default.
stops.campa: Out of the AOL job and back in California, he sits down with Ben Horowitz, Tim Howes, and In Sik Rhee and they agree to sell computing itself: servers, storage, and the running of them, rented by the month to companies that would otherwise have to buy the machines. The word for this in 1999 is managed hosting. The word for it fifteen years later will be the cloud, and the market for it will be worth hundreds of billions of dollars. They are seven years early, which in this business is the same as being wrong.
sources: Marc Andreessen research dossier (Loudcloud founding narrative)
suggested_refs: Loudcloud's founding team: Andreessen, Ben Horowitz, Tim Howes, In Sik Rhee

stops.name: Sunnyvale, the hosting business sold and the company renamed
stops.date_confidence: Attested that Loudcloud sold its managed-services business to Electronic Data Systems for $63.5 million in cash in 2002 and renamed itself Opsware, with Andreessen as chairman and Horowitz as chief executive (Wikipedia, 'Opsware' and 'Ben Horowitz'). The March 2001 initial public offering into the dot-com crash is attested in the dossier's company history and is folded into this stop rather than given its own. Month and day are defaults. Coordinates corrected from the pool's 37.3894, -122.0203, about 1.05 km off, to 599 North Mathilda Avenue, Sunnyvale, per Nominatim.
stops.campa: Loudcloud goes public in March 2001, into the crash rather than the boom, and the shares behave accordingly. The company is burning capital to run other people's machines. So they sell the machines: the whole managed-services business goes to Electronic Data Systems for sixty-three and a half million dollars, and what is left is the software Loudcloud wrote to automate its own data centers, which turns out to be the valuable part. The remainder renames itself Opsware. Horowitz runs it; Andreessen takes the chair.
suggested_refs: The EDS purchase of Loudcloud's managed-services business, 2002, and the founding of Opsware

stops.name: Palo Alto, Ning and the networks people build themselves
stops.date_confidence: Attested that Andreessen co-founded Ning with Gina Bianchini and served as its chief technology officer (University of Illinois Distributed Museum, fetched directly; dossier company history). The 2004 founding date, the 2005 launch, the Palo Alto location, and the roughly $150 million Glam Media purchase in 2011 come from the dossier and standard technology-press accounts and were not independently re-fetched; month and day are defaults.
stops.campa: With Gina Bianchini he starts Ning, which is a tool for making a social network the way a word processor is a tool for making a document: anyone can raise one, name it, and run it. It launches in 2005, a year after Facebook, and it takes the opposite bet, that people want many small networks of their own rather than one large one belonging to somebody else. The bet loses. Glam Media buys Ning in 2011, mostly in stock, for a figure reported around a hundred and fifty million dollars.
sources: University of Illinois Distributed Museum, exhibit page on Marc Andreessen
Marc Andreessen research dossier (Ning company history)
suggested_refs: Ning and Gina Bianchini's platform for user-created social networks, 2005-2011

stops.name: Stanford, the New Year's Eve dinner
stops.date_confidence: Attested that Andreessen and Laura Arrillaga met at a New Year's Eve dinner and married in 2006 (Wikipedia, 'Marc Andreessen', which says the dinner was organized by the former chief executive of eHarmony). The venue of the dinner is unknown; the pin is the Knight Management Center of the Stanford Graduate School of Business, corrected from the pool's 37.4275, -122.1697, and stands as the institutional anchor for Laura Arrillaga-Andreessen rather than as the site of anything described here. Month and day are the New Year's Eve dating rounded to the following day.
stops.campa: He meets Laura Arrillaga at a New Year's Eve dinner arranged by the former head of a dating company, which is the kind of detail the valley finds funny about itself. She teaches philanthropy at Stanford; her father, John Arrillaga, built a great deal of the physical Silicon Valley, the low tilt-up buildings the companies sit in. They marry that same year, about nine months later. The marriage joins the man who made the software layer to the family that poured the concrete under it.
sources: Marc Andreessen research dossier (Arrillaga family background)
suggested_refs: Laura Arrillaga-Andreessen's teaching and philanthropy work at Stanford
John Arrillaga's Silicon Valley real-estate development

stops.name: Palo Alto, Hewlett-Packard buys Opsware
stops.date_confidence: Attested as to the announcement date and terms: Wikipedia, 'Opsware', gives $14.25 per share in cash, $1.65 billion in total, announced July 2007, with the deal closing on 21 September 2007. The pool's $1.6 billion is corrected to $1.65 billion. Coordinates corrected from the pool's 37.4059, -122.1149, about 3 km off in south-central Palo Alto, to Hewlett-Packard headquarters at 3000 Hanover Street, per Nominatim.
stops.campa: Hewlett-Packard offers fourteen dollars and twenty-five cents a share in cash for Opsware, one billion six hundred and fifty million dollars for the automation software that was originally written only so Loudcloud could run its own machines with fewer people. What is bought is the leftover, the tool the company made for itself while failing at the business it meant to be in. Andreessen has now built and sold three companies. The deal closes on the twenty-first of September, 2007.
suggested_refs: The Hewlett-Packard acquisition of Opsware, announced 23 July 2007, closed 21 September 2007

segments.name: Sand Hill Road: The Firm and the Boards

stops.name: Menlo Park, the Facebook board seat
stops.date_confidence: The June 2008 board join is the dossier's date and is repeated in encyclopedia summaries; Meta's own investor-relations page was not fetched this session to confirm the month, so this is tagged as reconstruction on the date and attested on the substance of his long board service. The pin is 1 Hacker Way, Menlo Park, which is Meta's address from 2011 onward; in June 2008 the company was still in Palo Alto, and the pin marks the company rather than the room he joined.
stops.campa: He joins the board of Facebook, a company then four years old and run by a founder half his age. Two years earlier, by his own later telling, he had advised that founder to refuse a billion dollars from Yahoo and keep the company. He holds the seat through every phase that follows: the offering, the mobile turn, Cambridge Analytica, the change of the corporate name, the shareholder actions. The company's 2026 proxy statement still lists him as a director, eighteen years on.
sources: Marc Andreessen research dossier (June 2008 board join; Meta 2026 proxy statement)
suggested_refs: The 2006 Yahoo offer for Facebook and Andreessen's reported advice to refuse it

stops.name: San Jose, the eBay board seat
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day. The eBay Inc. investor-relations press release, 'Marc Andreessen Joins eBay Inc.'s Board of Directors' (investors.ebayinc.com), fetched directly in research, confirms the effective date of 30 September 2008 and the San Jose headquarters at 2145 Hamilton Avenue.
stops.campa: eBay announces that Marc Andreessen has joined its board of directors, effective the thirtieth of September. The company owns Skype, which it bought for two and a half billion dollars and has never worked out what to do with. Andreessen sits on the board that will decide what happens to it. Within a year he will also be a partner in the group that buys it. What that arrangement is called depends on who is describing it. Carl Icahn describes it in 2014, at length and in public.
sources: eBay Inc. investor relations press release, 'Marc Andreessen Joins eBay Inc.'s Board of Directors', 30 September 2008
suggested_refs: eBay Inc. headquarters, 2145 Hamilton Avenue, San Jose

stops.name: Menlo Park, Andreessen Horowitz
stops.date_confidence: Attested. Wikipedia, 'Andreessen Horowitz', gives the firm's announcement on 6 July 2009 with a first fund of about $300 million, founded with Ben Horowitz. Coordinates corrected from the pool's 37.421, -122.1988 and from the afterlife lens's still worse 37.453, -122.1817, both of which disagree with each other; the Nominatim value for Andreessen Horowitz, 2865 Sand Hill Road, Menlo Park is used here.
stops.campa: He and Horowitz open a venture firm on Sand Hill Road with a first fund of three hundred million dollars and a thesis about who should be running companies, which is founders. It is built as an institution rather than as a partnership of a few men with a checkbook: recruiters, marketers, a policy shop, a press operation. Andreessen has been publishing the argument since 2007, in a run of posts telling founders what a startup is for. Within a decade the firm is one of the largest in the industry.
stops.quote: The only thing that matters is getting to product/market fit.
stops.quote_source: Marc Andreessen, 'The Pmarca Guide to Startups, Part 4: The only thing that matters', 2007, republished at pmarchive.com
sources: pmarchive.com, 'The Pmarca Guide to Startups, Part 4'
